title: The Minor iv Chord (Modal Interchange in Major Keys)

instant_card.vibe: Bittersweet nostalgic yearning, sudden emotional lift
instant_card.hero_move: Hold the chord root, then slide your finger 1 fret down from the key's Major 3rd to the Minor 3rd on the G or B string.
twin_songs: Wake Me Up When September Ends (Green Day)
instant_card.target_degree_motion: 3 -> b3 (E -> Eb in key of G)

the_musical_why: In a major key, the IV chord (like C in G major) is completely diatonic and happy. Turning it into a minor chord (Cm) introduces the Eb note from the parallel minor scale. This Eb acts as a powerful voice-leading gravitational pull because it sits just a single half step above D (the 5th of the home key), creating a tear-jerking bittersweet resolution.
caged_anchors: Root-6 E-Shape: B-string Fret 8 (Eb in Cm)
Root-5 A-Shape: D-string Fret 1 or G-string Fret 5 (Eb in Cm)
soloing_scales: Minor Pentatonic over the iv chord
Melodic Minor built on the iv root
practice_drill: 1) Set up a G - B - C - Cm backing loop. 2) Play your standard G Major Pentatonic over G and C. 3) The exact moment Cm hits, slide your index or middle finger down one half-step to land squarely on the Eb note.

title: Secondary Dominant V/vi (The Major III Pulling to Minor vi)

instant_card.vibe: Dramatic Spanish tension, suspenseful build-up before falling into melancholy
instant_card.hero_move: Target the major 3rd of the III chord — it is a foreign sharp note that pulls up a half step into the root of the vi chord.
twin_songs: Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out
instant_card.target_degree_motion: #5 of key / 3 of III resolving up a half-step to root of vi (D# -> E)

the_musical_why: In G major, the 3rd chord is normally diatonic B minor. Changing it to B major or B7 turns it into a secondary dominant pointing straight at E minor (vi). The secret spice is the D# note inside B7 — D# is not in the G major scale! It functions as a sharp leading tone that aggressively begs to resolve upward by one half-step into E.
caged_anchors: Root-5 A-Shape: D-string Fret 4 (F#) and G-string Fret 4 (B) with B-string Fret 4 (D#)
Root-6 E-Shape: G-string Fret 8 (D#)
soloing_scales: Harmonic Minor of the target vi chord (E Harmonic Minor)
B Mixolydian b9 b13 (5th mode of Harmonic Minor)
practice_drill: 1) Loop G -> B7 -> Em. 2) Over B7, target the D# note on G-string Fret 8. 3) On the downbeat of Em, slide your finger up one single fret to E (G-string Fret 9).

title: Tritone Substitution (The Chromatic Slide Dominant)

instant_card.vibe: Sleek, smoky jazz sophistication, chromatic sliding gravity
instant_card.hero_move: Play the dominant 7th chord built 1 half-step above your target chord — the bass slides down while guide tones resolve naturally.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Bass drops chromatic half step (Db -> C) while 3rd and 7th pivot seamlessly

the_musical_why: Every dominant 7th chord is propelled by its unstable tritone interval between the 3rd and 7th. In G7, the guide tones are B and F (6 semitones apart). If you travel 6 semitones away across the circle of fifths to Db7, its guide tones are F and Cb (enharmonic to B)! Because G7 and Db7 share the exact same guide-tone engine, Db7 can replace G7, producing a chromatic descending bassline (Db to C) that sounds ultra-smooth.
caged_anchors: Root-5 A-Shape: Fret 4 on A-string (Db), Fret 3 on D-string (F), Fret 4 on G-string (B/Cb)
Root-6 E-Shape: Fret 9 on Low E-string (Db)
practice_drill: 1) In a standard Dm7 -> G7 -> Cmaj7 progression, swap G7 for Db7. 2) Solo with D Dorian over Dm7. 3) Over Db7, outline the Db7 arpeggio landing on F (fret 6 on B string) before resolving to E on Cmaj7.

title: The Blues I7 to IV7 Shift (Major vs Minor Pentatonic Harmony)

instant_card.vibe: Sweet soulful vocal sweetness on I, gritty raw biting drive on IV
instant_card.hero_move: Play sweet Major Pentatonic / B.B. King box on the I chord, then switch to raw Minor Pentatonic on the IV chord.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Major 3rd of I chord (C# in A7) shifts to b7 of IV chord (C natural in D7)

the_musical_why: In a blues in A, the I chord is A7 (containing the sweet major 3rd C#). Playing A Major Pentatonic sounds gorgeous over A7. But when the band shifts to the IV chord (D7), the D7 chord contains a C natural (its dominant 7th)! If you keep playing your sweet C# note over D7, it clashes hideously against the D7 harmony. Shifting to A Minor Pentatonic introduces the C natural, perfectly targeting the dominant soul of the IV chord.
caged_anchors: B.B. King Box: Strings 1, 2, 3 around Fret 10 (Root on B string Fret 10)
Box 1 Minor Pentatonic: Fret 5 across all 6 strings
soloing_scales: Major Pentatonic / B.B. King Box over I7
Minor Blues Scale over IV7 and V7
practice_drill: 1) Fire up an A Blues 12-bar backing track. 2) On bars 1-4 (A7), solo strictly in the B.B. King box (frets 9-12 on strings 1-3). 3) On bar 5 when D7 hits, drop into Box 1 at fret 5 and bend the b3 (C) slightly microtonally.

title: Hendrix & Mayer R&B Chord Embellishments (Hammer-on Fills)

instant_card.vibe: Silky, fluid neo-soul and vintage R&B cascade without moving hand position
instant_card.hero_move: Fret a root-anchor with your thumb or barre, and use your pinky and ring fingers to hammer-on the 4th, 9th, or 6th degree.
twin_songs: Slow Dancing in a Burning Room (John Mayer)

the_musical_why: Jimi Hendrix, Curtis Mayfield, and John Mayer blurred the line between rhythm guitar and soloing. Instead of strumming static barre chords, they keep the chord grip anchored with the fretting hand while hammering decorative scale tones (the 4th, 9th, and 6th). These hammer-on diads create vocal-like ornamentations that make rhythm guitar sound like an orchestral lead.
caged_anchors: CAGED Root-6 E-Shape: Strings 3 & 4 hammer-ons at frets 7 to 9
CAGED Root-5 A-Shape: Strings 2 & 3 hammer-ons at frets 5 to 7
practice_drill: 1) Grip an A-major CAGED E-shape at fret 5 (thumb on Low E fret 5). 2) Hammer your ring finger on the G string from fret 6 (Major 3rd) to fret 7 (4th degree). 3) Pull back off to fret 6 to complete the classic Little Wing sigh.

title: The Backdoor Progression bVII7 to I (Soul & Neo-Soul Cadence)

instant_card.vibe: Silky, unexpected soul warmth, soaring resolution into light
instant_card.hero_move: Target the b7 of the bVII7 chord — it sits just a half step above the 5th of your target chord.
twin_songs: If I Ain't Got You (Alicia Keys)
instant_card.target_degree_motion: b7 of bVII7 (Ab in Bb7) slides down a half step to 5th of I (G in Cmaj7)

the_musical_why: In a traditional V7 -> I cadence (G7 to C), the leading tone B pulls up to C. In the backdoor cadence, we substitute the minor iv (Fm7) and its dominant partner bVII7 (Bb7). The Bb7 chord contains Ab (its dominant 7th) and D (its 3rd). Instead of pulling upward, the Ab smoothly glides down a half step into G (the 5th of Cmaj7). It feels like entering the home room through the backdoor garden instead of the front porch.
caged_anchors: CAGED Root-6 E-Shape: Fret 6 on Low E-string (Bb7) with Fret 9 on B-string (Ab)
CAGED Root-5 A-Shape: Fret 1 on A-string (Bb7)
practice_drill: 1) Loop Fm7 -> Bb7 -> Cmaj7. 2) Over Bb7, fret Ab on B-string Fret 9. 3) On Cmaj7, slide down 1 fret to G on Fret 8 and let it sing.

title: The ii-V-I Guide Tone Cascade (The Jazz Engine)

instant_card.vibe: Classic, effortless storytelling with endless forward momentum
instant_card.hero_move: The 7th of chord 1 falls down 1 fret to become the 3rd of chord 2; then the 7th of chord 2 falls down 1 fret to become the 3rd of chord 3.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Cascading 7th -> 3rd half-step drops: C -> B (on G7), then F -> E (on Cmaj7)

the_musical_why: The ii-V-I is the foundation of jazz and American popular song. The entire harmonic engine runs on two notes: the 3rd and the 7th (the guide tones). When moving from Dm7 to G7, the 7th of Dm7 (C) falls by a single half-step to the 3rd of G7 (B). When moving from G7 to Cmaj7, the 7th of G7 (F) falls by a single half-step to the 3rd of Cmaj7 (E). By targeting these half-step handshakes, you sound like you are outlining the chords without strumming them.
caged_anchors: Root-5 / Root-6 Guide Tone Shells: Strings 3 & 4 at frets 9 to 10
Strings 1 & 2 at frets 5 to 7
soloing_scales: D Dorian -> G Mixolydian -> C Major
practice_drill: 1) Set up Dm7 - G7 - Cmaj7. 2) Play ONLY two notes per chord on strings 3 and 4 (the guide tones). 3) Watch your fingers descend by 1 fret on each change like clockwork.

title: Superimposed Triads (Instant 9ths, 11ths, and 13ths)
roman_numeral: Upper Triads over Imaj7, ii7, and V7

instant_card.vibe: Sophisticated, airy modern guitar sound without memorizing complex scales
instant_card.hero_move: Play a simple 3-note minor triad off the 3rd of any major 7th chord (e.g. play Em over Cmaj7) to instantly unlock the major 9th.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Triad root over chord 3rd (Em: E-G-B gives 3-5-7; Bm: B-D-F# gives 7-9-#11)

the_musical_why: Pro guitarists rarely play basic root-position chords during a solo. Instead, they superimpose simple triads over the bass note. Over a Cmaj7 chord, playing an Em triad (E-G-B) outlines the 3rd, 5th, and 7th. Playing a Bm triad (B-D-F#) outlines the 7th, 9th, and #11 (Lydian sound). Because your fingers already know basic triad shapes anywhere on the neck, this instantly unlocks modern fusion sounds without learning 10 new modes.
caged_anchors: Top 3 Strings (1-2-3): Em triad at frets 7-8-7 or 12-12-12
Middle Strings (2-3-4): Bm triad at frets 7-7-7
practice_drill: 1) Loop a static Cmaj7 or C bass drone. 2) Solo using ONLY the E minor triad (E, G, B) across strings 1, 2, and 3. 3) Notice how it sounds like an airy, sophisticated Cmaj7 extension without touching the root note C.

title: Diminished 7th Passing Chords (The Symmetrical Glue)

instant_card.vibe: Old-school swing tension, chromatic connecting glue, dramatic lift
instant_card.hero_move: Slide the exact same 4-finger diminished grip up or down 3 frets — every note in the chord inverts symmetrically.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Bass climbs chromatically (#I -> ii) while diminished tones resolve inward

the_musical_why: A diminished 7th chord is built entirely of minor 3rd intervals (3 frets apart). Because it is perfectly symmetrical, moving any diminished 7th chord grip up or down by 3 frets yields the exact same notes in a different inversion! Furthermore, any diminished 7th chord is secretly a rootless dominant 7(b9) chord. In C major, playing C#dim7 between C and Dm gives a chromatic ascending bassline (C -> C# -> D) while acting as an A7(b9) secondary dominant resolving to Dm.
caged_anchors: 4-String Grip (Strings 1-4 or 2-5): Fret 4 on B, Fret 3 on G, Fret 5 on D, Fret 4 on A (C#dim7)
Move whole shape +3 frets to Fret 7, 10, 13
practice_drill: 1) Loop C -> C#dim7 -> Dm7 -> G7. 2) Over C#dim7, play a 4-note diminished arpeggio. 3) Slide the entire shape up 3 frets and play the exact same lick.

title: The Dorian vs Aeolian Modal Shift (The Major 6th Hero Note)

instant_card.vibe: Dorian = optimistic, uplifted Santana/Pink Floyd groove. Aeolian = tragic, dark classic sadness.
instant_card.hero_move: To sound Dorian, target the Major 6th note (B in D Dorian, F# in A Dorian). To sound Aeolian, drop it 1 fret down to Minor 6th.
instant_card.target_degree_motion: Major 6th (sweet Dorian) vs Minor 6th (tragic Aeolian) 1-fret switch

the_musical_why: Both Dorian and Aeolian are minor modes with a minor 3rd and minor 7th. The single note that separates them is the 6th degree. Aeolian has a minor 6th (F in A minor), which feels tragic and heavy. Dorian raises that note to a Major 6th (F# in A minor), which instantly removes the gloom and injects breezy, optimistic funk/rock flavor. When a progression has a major IV chord (like Am to D7), it is strictly Dorian, and targeting that raised 6th note is the secret to sounding like Carlos Santana.
caged_anchors: Root-6 Box 1: B-string Fret 7 (F# in A Dorian)
Root-5 Box: G-string Fret 11 (F# in A Dorian)
practice_drill: 1) Loop an Am7 to D7 groove. 2) Solo in A Minor Pentatonic at fret 5. 3) On the D7 chord, deliberately land on the F# note on B-string Fret 7 (the Major 6th) and add wide vibrato.
